title: Comparative advantage
examples: How does opportunity cost help decide who should specialize?
Can trade happen even if one country is better at everything?
What is the difference between absolute and comparative advantage?

explain.say: Today we explore comparative advantage in economics. This helps us know who should specialize in what.

items: Specialization means focusing on what you do best.
Trade allows everyone to benefit more.

explain.say: First we look at opportunity cost. It is what you give up to get something else. For example, making one pair of shoes means giving up two loaves of bread.

draw.text: Opportunity Cost: What you give up

explain.say: Next we compare opportunity cost ratios. If Country A gives up three cars for one tractor, that is their ratio. Country B might give up only two cars for that same tractor.

This leads us to comparative advantage. A country has a comparative advantage where its opportunity cost is lowest. Country B has the comparative advantage in tractors because they give up fewer cars.
The gains from trade show why specialization helps everyone. If both countries trade, they can consume more than they could alone. This is the benefit of trade.

In a real life example, think about a local bakery and a local printer. The bakery should specialize in bread because they know how to do it best. The printer should specialize in printing because they have the best equipment.

faq.q: What is the difference between absolute and comparative advantage?
faq.a: Absolute advantage means producing more using the same resources. Comparative advantage relates to the lower opportunity cost of producing something.
asks: Is it about who is best at everything?
Does it only use total output?

faq.q: Does every country have a comparative advantage?
faq.a: Yes, in any scenario involving two goods and two countries, there will be a comparative advantage in at least one good for each country.
asks: Is it possible for no one to have an advantage?

faq.q: How do I calculate the opportunity cost?
faq.a: You divide the amount of one good given up by the amount of the other good gained. Keep track of the ratios carefully.
asks: Is it just dividing the prices?
Do I use money or just quantities?

faq.q: What happens if countries trade based on comparative advantage?
faq.a: They can trade goods and services to achieve a total output level that is higher than if they produced everything themselves.
asks: Does trade always make things better?

faq.q: Can a country with smaller resources still benefit from trade?
faq.a: Yes, if the country specializes in what it does relatively best, it can trade for goods it cannot produce efficiently.

facts: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative foregone.
Comparative advantage exists where the opportunity cost is lowest.
Gains from trade occur when specialization and exchange take place.
Absolute advantage means producing more output than another party.

quiz.say: If making 1 car costs giving up 2 bags of wheat, and making 1 tractor costs giving up 4 bags of wheat, which good has the lower opportunity cost?
quiz.why: The car costs only 2 bags of wheat, which is less than the 4 bags needed for the tractor.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the ratios (2 to 1 vs 4 to 1) are clearly different.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the question asks to compare the cost of the two manufactured goods.
wrong.3: It is tempting because the tractor is a bigger item, suggesting a higher cost.

quiz.say: If Country A specializes in wheat and Country B specializes in cars, what is the main economic benefit?

options.show: Total consumption increases for both countries.
options.say: Total consumption increases for both countries.

options.show: The trade must be equal in value.
options.say: The trade must be equal in value.

options.show: The country with the largest absolute output wins.
options.say: The country with the largest absolute output wins.

options.show: The goods must be identical to trade.
options.say: The goods must be identical to trade.

quiz.why: By specializing, both countries can produce more overall than if they tried to produce everything themselves.

wrong.1: This is wrong because trade is based on comparative advantage, not necessarily an equal exchange value.
wrong.2: This is wrong because comparative advantage, not just size, determines who should specialize.
wrong.3: This is wrong because trade can happen between different types of goods and services.
